title: mwmap: A Complete Guide to Mapping Malawi in R
text:
mwmap is an R package that makes it easy to create accurate, professional maps of Malawi using nothing more than a few lines of R code. It bundles pre-processed spatial boundary data for every administrative level in the country — from the national border down to individual Traditional Authorities — and wraps that data in a family of functions that handle the tedious parts of GIS work for you: joining your spreadsheet data to map geometries, normalising inconsistent district name spellings, choosing colour scales, and producing figures that are ready to drop straight into a report or publication.

The package is built on top of ggplot2 and sf, the two most widely used R packages for data visualisation and spatial analysis respectively. If you already know ggplot2, you will feel immediately at home — every mwmap function returns a ggplot2 object, so you can add layers, themes, and scales using the familiar + operator.
You do not need to be a GIS expert to use mwmap. You do not need to download shapefiles, reproject coordinate systems, or understand spatial data formats. All of that is handled internally. What you bring is your district-level data — disease counts, survey estimates, economic indicators — and mwmap handles the cartographic heavy lifting.






NoteInstallation



mwmap is available on CRAN and can be installed in the usual way:
# Stable release from CRAN
install.packages("mwmap")

# Latest development version from GitHub
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("bitacanalytics/mwmap")
Once installed, load it alongside ggplot2:
library(mwmap)
library(ggplot2)




mwmap is organised into five functional groups. Understanding this structure helps you find the right function quickly.
Core mapping functions produce the base map canvas. You will almost always start with one of these before adding any data layers on top.
Data and joining functions are the bridge between your spreadsheet and the map geometry. They handle the spatial join, clean up district names, and report on how well your data matched the shapefile.
Layer functions add elements on top of an existing base map — highlighted districts, point locations, text labels. These are designed to be chained together using +.
Styling functions control colour scales and overall layout. The built-in palettes have been chosen to work well for the most common Malawi mapping use cases (health, agriculture, poverty, administration).
Utility functions are helpers you will use indirectly but that are also useful on their own — particularly for cleaning district name columns before a join.

mwmap function groups






Category
Functions




Core mapping
mw_map(), mw_regions(), mw_ta_map()


Data & joining
mw_join(), mw_choropleth(), mw_districts(), mw_districts_simple()


Map layers
mw_highlight(), mw_highlight_multi(), mw_points(), mw_labels(), mw_label_repel()


Styling
mw_layout(), scale_fill_mw(), get_mw_palette(), get_mw_palettes(), view_mw_palettes()


Utilities
mw_clean_names(), mw_suggest_matches()



The package also ships five built-in spatial datasets. These are sf objects — essentially data frames where one column contains polygon geometry — sourced from the Malawi Spatial Data Platform (MASDAP) and pre-processed for use in R.

Spatial datasets bundled in mwmap







Dataset
Description
Polygons

National boundary of Malawi
1

title: mwmap: A Complete Guide to Mapping Malawi in R
text:
1.1 Your first map
The fastest way to get started is to call mw_map() with no arguments. This produces a clean, grey district-level outline of Malawi in a single line of code.

library(mwmap)
library(ggplot2)

mw_map()







Figure 1: A minimal Malawi map produced by mw_map() with no arguments.





What you get back is a standard ggplot2 object — the same kind of object you get from calling ggplot(). This is important because it means you can immediately extend the map using any ggplot2 syntax you already know. Want to add a title? Use labs(). Want to change the background colour? Use theme(). Want to add a second layer of points or polygons? Just use +.

mw_map() +
  labs(
    title = "Malawi Administrative Districts",
    caption = "Source: MASDAP / Department of Surveys"
  )







Figure 2: The same map with a title and caption added using standard ggplot2 labs().

title: mwmap: A Complete Guide to Mapping Malawi in R
text:
1.2 Understanding administrative levels
Malawi’s administrative geography has four nested levels. mwmap bundles data for all four, and you switch between them using the level argument in mw_map().

Level 0 is the national boundary — useful as a reference outline or backdrop behind other data.
Level 1 shows the three regions: Northern, Central, and Southern. Regional comparisons — vaccination coverage, food security — are a natural fit for this level.
Level 2 is the default and the most commonly used level. Malawi’s 28 districts are the primary unit for government statistics, health surveillance, and most national surveys.
Level 3 shows Traditional Authorities, the sub-district units governed by traditional leaders. This is the finest grain available in the package and is useful for local-level planning and community health work.

mw_map(level = 0) + labs(title = "Level 0 — National boundary")
mw_map(level = 1) + labs(title = "Level 1 — Three regions")
mw_map(level = 2) + labs(title = "Level 2 — 28 districts (default)")
mw_map(level = 3) + labs(title = "Level 3 — Traditional Authorities")









Figure 3: All four administrative levels available in mwmap. Level 2 (districts) is the default.











Figure 4: All four administrative levels available in mwmap. Level 2 (districts) is the default.













Figure 5: All four administrative levels available in mwmap. Level 2 (districts) is the default.











Figure 6: All four administrative levels available in mwmap. Level 2 (districts) is the default.






Notice how level 3 is considerably more detailed. Because Traditional Authority boundaries are complex, rendering the full level-3 map is slower than the other levels. If you only need a subset of TAs — for example, those in a single district — use mw_ta_map(districts = "Lilongwe") rather than mw_map(level = 3) to keep rendering fast.

title: mwmap: A Complete Guide to Mapping Malawi in R
section: 1.3 Filtering to a region or set of districts
text:
1.3 Filtering to a region or set of districts
You will often want to focus on a subset of the country rather than mapping everything at once. mwmap gives you two built-in filters:

region accepts the full region name ("Northern", "Central", "Southern") or a single-letter shortcut ("n", "c", "s").
districts accepts a character vector of district names. Matching is case-insensitive.

When you filter to a region, mw_map() automatically crops the bounding box so the selected area fills the plot. You do not need to adjust any axis limits manually.
# Shortcut "s" is equivalent to "Southern"
mw_map(region = "s") +
  labs(title = "Southern Region")

# Show Lilongwe and its neighbouring districts
mw_map(districts = c("Lilongwe", "Dowa", "Dedza", "Ntcheu", "Mchinji")) +
  labs(title = "Lilongwe and Neighbouring Districts")









Figure 7: Filtering to a single region (left) or a custom set of districts (right).











Figure 8: Filtering to a single region (left) or a custom set of districts (right).

title: mwmap: A Complete Guide to Mapping Malawi in R
text:
2.1 mw_map() — the main workhorse
mw_map() is the central function in the package. Nearly every workflow starts here. It is designed to be useful at both extremes — a single call with no arguments produces a clean outline, while a heavily parameterised call can produce a complete choropleth with highlights, labels, and lake overlay in one step.
The table below covers the most important arguments. A complete reference is available via ?mw_map.

Key mw_map() arguments







Argument
Default
What it does




level
2
Administrative level: 0 = country, 1 = regions, 2 = districts, 3 = TAs


data
NULL
A data frame or sf object with values to display


fill
NULL
Column name (as a string) to use for choropleth fill colour


fill_color
"#f0f0f0"
Solid fill colour when no fill column is provided


lakes
FALSE
Whether to overlay the three major lakes


lake_color
"#9ecae1"
Fill colour for lakes


borders
TRUE
Whether to draw polygon borders


border_color
"#333333"
Border colour


border_size
0.3
Border line width


region
NULL
Restrict map to one region


districts
NULL
Restrict map to named districts


label_districts
FALSE
Add district name labels at centroids


label_size
3
Size of district labels


highlight_districts
NULL
Districts to draw with a bold coloured border


highlight_border_color
"#E41A1C"
Colour of the highlight border


highlight_fill
NA
Fill colour for highlighted districts (NA = transparent)


interactive
FALSE
Return a plotly interactive map instead of ggplot2


title, subtitle, caption
NULL
Map text elements




2.1.1 Adding the major lakes
Malawi is defined by water as much as by its land. Lake Malawi covers roughly a fifth of the country’s total area, and Lakes Malombe and Chilwa are significant features in the south. For most maps, adding the lakes makes the geography immediately recognisable to a Malawian audience and gives the reader an important spatial reference point.
Set lakes = TRUE to overlay them. You can adjust the fill colour with lake_color and the border with lake_border_color.

mw_map(
  lakes = TRUE,
  lake_color = "#6BAED6",
  lake_border_color = "#3182BD"
) +
  labs(title = "Malawi — Districts and Major Lakes")







Figure 9: District map with major lakes overlaid. The lakes are stored as a separate sf dataset (major_lakes) and drawn on top of the district polygons.







2.1.2 Highlighting specific districts
mw_map() has built-in support for drawing attention to specific districts without needing a separate mw_highlight() layer. Use highlight_districts to name the districts you want to emphasise.
By default, the highlight draws a bold red border around the named districts. You can customise the border colour, border width, and fill colour. Setting highlight_fill = NA (the default) makes the fill transparent — only the bold border draws attention while the underlying fill colour remains visible.

mw_map(
  highlight_districts = c("Lilongwe", "Blantyre", "Mzimba"),
  highlight_border_color = "#E41A1C",
  highlight_border_size = 1.5,
  highlight_fill = "#FEEDDE"
) +
  labs(
    title = "Major Urban Districts",
    caption = "Highlighted: Lilongwe, Blantyre, Mzimba"
  )







Figure 10: Three major urban districts highlighted with a bold coloured border and a light orange fill.







2.1.3 Adding district name labels
Set label_districts = TRUE to add each district name at the centroid of its polygon. Labels that would overlap are automatically suppressed. For finer control — labelling only specific districts, changing the font, or using ggrepel for non-overlapping placement — use the standalone mw_labels() function described in Section 4.4.

mw_map(
  fill_color = "#f7f7f7",
  border_color = "grey60",
  label_districts = TRUE,
  label_size = 2.5,
  label_color = "#333333"
) +
  labs(title = "Malawi District Names")







Figure 11: All 28 district names added via label_districts = TRUE.

title: mwmap: A Complete Guide to Mapping Malawi in R
text:
2.2 mw_regions() — regional overview
mw_regions() is a convenience function that aggregates the 28 district polygons into the three administrative regions and plots them. Internally it calls dplyr::group_by() and sf::st_union() to dissolve district boundaries, so you do not need to pre-process the data yourself.
Use this function when your analysis is at the regional level — comparing Northern, Central, and Southern on some indicator — or when you need a clean regional overview to orient the reader at the start of a report.
The region_colors argument accepts a named vector where the names are "Northern", "Central", and "Southern". This makes it straightforward to encode data values as fill colours by pre-computing the colour for each region and passing the result in.

mw_regions(
  region_colors = c(
    "Northern" = "#E41A1C",
    "Central" = "#377EB8",
    "Southern" = "#4DAF4A"
  ),
  labels = TRUE,
  label_size = 5,
  label_color = "white",
  label_face = "bold",
  lakes = TRUE
) +
  labs(title = "Administrative Regions of Malawi")







Figure 12: The three administrative regions with distinct colours, name labels, and the major lakes overlaid.





Notice that labels = TRUE places each region name at the geometric centroid of the dissolved polygon. For the Southern Region — which wraps around Lake Malawi — the centroid may not look perfectly centred visually, but it is the mathematical centre of the polygon.

title: mwmap: A Complete Guide to Mapping Malawi in R
text:
2.3 mw_ta_map() — traditional authorities
Traditional Authorities (TAs) are the sub-district administrative units in Malawi, each governed by a customary chief. The package includes boundaries for approximately 250 TAs sourced from MASDAP. mw_ta_map() is a dedicated function for rendering these boundaries, with several features designed for working at this fine scale.
The most important argument is districts. Rendering all 250 TAs at once is slow and the resulting map is very dense. It is almost always better to filter to the district or districts you care about. When you do, mw_ta_map() also draws the district boundary on top of the TA polygons by default (district_border = TRUE), which helps the reader understand where the selected TAs sit within the broader geography.

mw_ta_map(
  border_color = "grey70",
  border_size = 0.15,
  district_border = TRUE,
  district_border_color = "#E41A1C",
  district_border_size = 0.6
) +
  labs(
    title = "Traditional Authorities of Malawi",
    caption = "Thin grey = TA boundaries · Thick red = district boundaries"
  )







Figure 13: All Traditional Authorities. Thin grey lines are TA boundaries; thicker red lines are district boundaries drawn on top.





Filtering to specific districts dramatically improves readability and speed.

mw_ta_map(
  districts = c("Lilongwe", "Dowa"),
  labels = TRUE,
  label_size = 2,
  label_color = "#333333",
  district_border_color = "black",
  district_border_size = 0.9
) +
  labs(title = "Traditional Authorities — Lilongwe and Dowa")







Figure 14: TAs in just two districts. Filtering with the districts argument makes the map much more readable and faster to render.











Tipmw_ta_map() vs mw_map(level = 3)



Both produce TA-level maps but are designed for different situations. Use mw_map(level = 3) when you want to layer TA boundaries on top of other mw_map() features like fill data, highlights, or points. Use mw_ta_map() when you want the dedicated district-border overlay and the districts filter, which are specific to this function.

title: mwmap: A Complete Guide to Mapping Malawi in R
text:
3.1 Quick route — mw_choropleth()
mw_choropleth() is designed for speed. You pass it a data frame, the name of the column you want to map (unquoted, like a tidyverse verb), and optionally a palette name. It handles the join, the scale, and the plot in a single call.
The key arguments are:

data — your data frame. It must contain a column of district names.
value — the column to map, passed unquoted (e.g. malaria_cases, not "malaria_cases").
district_col — the name of the district name column in your data. Defaults to "district".
palette — one of the 25 named mwmap palettes. Defaults to "health".
scale_type — "auto" (the default) detects whether your variable is numeric (continuous scale) or a factor (discrete scale).
lakes — whether to overlay major lakes.
title, subtitle, caption — text elements for the map.

To demonstrate, we will use a simulated dataset of malaria indicators for all 28 districts. This same dataset is reused throughout the rest of this guide.

# Reading simulated district-level health data for all 28 districts

health_data <- read_csv("Malaria_data.csv")

head(health_data)





district
malaria_cases
population




Lilongwe
12450
2300000


Blantyre
9870
1800000


Mzimba
6540
940000


Zomba
7820
1050000


Mzuzu City
2310
220000


Kasungu
4560
780000







mw_choropleth(
  health_data,
  malaria_cases,
  palette = "malaria",
  title = "Reported Malaria Cases by District",
  subtitle = "Simulated data for illustration",
  caption = "Source: Simulated · mwmap package"
)







Figure 15: A basic choropleth of malaria case counts. Note how Lilongwe and Blantyre dominate simply because they have the largest populations — not necessarily the highest risk.






3.1.1 Why you should map rates, not raw counts
The map above shows Lilongwe and Blantyre with the highest case counts. But those are also Malawi’s two most populous districts — of course they have more cases. This is a classic pitfall in choropleth mapping. A map of raw counts often tells you more about population distribution than about the phenomenon you are trying to understand.
The solution is to compute a rate — dividing the count by the population to put all districts on a comparable footing. A rate per 1,000 population is a standard epidemiological measure.

health_data$rate_per_1000 <- round(
  health_data$malaria_cases / health_data$population * 1000,
  1
)

mw_choropleth(
  health_data,
  rate_per_1000,
  palette = "malaria",
  title = "Malaria Incidence Rate by District",
  subtitle = "Cases per 1,000 population · Simulated data",
  legend_title = "Rate per 1,000",
  caption = "Source: Simulated · mwmap package",
  n_breaks = 5
)







Figure 16: The same data expressed as a rate per 1,000 population. The geographic pattern is now very different — smaller, more rural districts may show higher burden than the urban centres.





Comparing these two maps is instructive. The count map is dominated by the two big cities; the rate map may look completely different, revealing high-burden districts that were invisible in the count map.


3.1.2 Categorical (discrete) choropleths
Not all variables are continuous numbers. Sometimes you want to map a category — risk tier, intervention group, funding status. When your variable is a factor, mw_choropleth() detects this automatically and switches to a discrete colour scale. We use cut() with ordered_result = TRUE to create an ordered factor, which tells the colour scale to arrange the legend from low to high.

health_data$risk_tier <- cut(
  health_data$rate_per_1000,
  breaks = c(0, 4, 7, 10, 15, Inf),
  labels = c("Very Low", "Low", "Medium", "High", "Very High"),
  right = TRUE
)

mw_choropleth(
  health_data,
  risk_tier,
  palette = "health",
  title = "Malaria Risk Tier by District",
  legend_title = "Risk Level",
  caption = "Source: Simulated · mwmap package"
)







Figure 17: A categorical choropleth. mw_choropleth() detects the factor variable automatically and uses a discrete scale.

title: mwmap: A Complete Guide to Mapping Malawi in R
text:
3.2 Flexible route — mw_join() + mw_map()
When you need more control than mw_choropleth() offers — a custom scale, additional layers, multiple fills — the two-step approach gives you full flexibility. The idea is simple:

Join your data to the map geometry using mw_join(), producing an sf object where every district row is enriched with your data columns.
Plot that joined sf object using mw_map(data = ..., fill = ...).

Because the result of step 1 is an sf object, you can then add any ggplot2 scales, mw_highlight() layers, mw_points() layers, or custom themes.

# Step 1: join your data frame to the district polygons
joined <- mw_join(
  data = health_data,
  district_col = "district",
  quiet = TRUE
)

# Step 2: pass the joined sf object to mw_map()
mw_map(
  data = joined,
  fill = "rate_per_1000",
  lakes = TRUE,
  border_color = "white",
  border_size = 0.4,
  title = "Malaria Incidence Rate",
  subtitle = "Cases per 1,000 population"
) +
  scale_fill_mw(
    palette = "malaria",
    name = "Rate per 1,000",
    na.value = "grey80"
  )







Figure 18: The two-step mw_join() + mw_map() workflow. Joining first gives you full control over scales and additional layers.






3.2.1 How mw_join() works
mw_join() is more than a simple merge. Under the hood it does several things that make it far more robust than calling dplyr::left_join() directly:
Name standardisation. Before attempting to match, mw_join() passes all district names through mw_clean_names() automatically. This normalises capitalisation, removes trailing words like “District” or “TA”, and fixes known variants (for example, “Nkhata Bay” becomes “Nkhatabay” to match the shapefile). Most of the time your data will join cleanly without any pre-processing.
A matching report. By default (verbose = TRUE), mw_join() prints a summary showing how many of your districts matched the shapefile, which ones did not match, and — for the unmatched ones — a list of suggested alternatives based on string similarity. This is invaluable for catching typos early.
A left join by default. mw_join() keeps all 28 district rows from the shapefile regardless of whether your data has a value for that district (keep_all = TRUE). Districts with no data appear grey on the map. This prevents the common mistake of accidentally hiding districts with missing data.

# Run mw_join() without quiet = TRUE to see the matching report.
# This is especially useful when working with a new dataset for the first time.
joined_verbose <- mw_join(
  data.frame(
    district = c("lilongwe", "BLANTYRE", "Mzimba", "Zomba City"),
    value = c(120, 200, 85, 60)
  ),
  district_col = "district"
)
# mw_join() will tell you that "Zomba City" did not match and suggest "Zomba"

title: mwmap: A Complete Guide to Mapping Malawi in R
text:
4.1 mw_highlight() — draw attention to districts
mw_highlight() overlays a coloured fill or bold outline on specific districts. It is useful whenever you want to direct the reader’s eye to particular areas — the districts covered by a programme, the ones that exceed a threshold, the capital and major cities.
The key arguments are:

districts — district names to highlight (case-insensitive).
fill — the fill colour. Defaults to "red".
color — the border colour. Defaults to "black".
alpha — fill transparency, from 0 (invisible) to 1 (opaque).
size — border line width.
outline_only — if TRUE, suppresses the fill and draws only the border. Ideal for adding emphasis on top of a choropleth without obscuring data values.
label — if TRUE, adds district name labels inside highlighted areas.


mw_map(fill_color = "#f0f0f0", border_color = "grey70") +
  mw_highlight(
    districts = c("Salima", "Nkhotakota", "Mangochi"),
    fill = "#FEC44F",
    color = "#E6550D",
    alpha = 0.85,
    size = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Lakeshore Districts of Malawi",
    subtitle = "Salima · Nkhotakota · Mangochi"
  )







Figure 19: Three lakeshore districts highlighted with a gold fill. The highlight layer sits on top of the base map and is styled independently.






4.1.1 Using outline_only = TRUE on a choropleth
When you have a choropleth showing continuous values, a solid fill highlight would cover the data. The outline_only option draws just the border, adding visual emphasis without obscuring the underlying colours.

mw_choropleth(health_data, rate_per_1000, palette = "health", quiet = TRUE) +
  mw_highlight(
    districts = c("Lilongwe", "Blantyre"),
    outline_only = TRUE,
    color = "#E41A1C",
    size = 1.2
  ) +
  labs(caption = "Red outline = major urban centres")







Figure 20: A bold outline highlight layered on top of a choropleth. The fill values remain fully visible.

title: mwmap: A Complete Guide to Mapping Malawi in R
section: 4.2 mw_highlight_multi() — a different colour per district
text:
4.2 mw_highlight_multi() — a different colour per district
When you want to highlight several districts but give each one a distinct colour — to show which programme operates in each area, or to indicate different intervention types — mw_highlight_multi() accepts a named vector where the names are district names and the values are colours.

mw_map(fill_color = "#f7f7f7", border_color = "grey70") +
  mw_highlight_multi(
    c(
      "Lilongwe" = "#377EB8",
      "Blantyre" = "#E41A1C",
      "Mzuzu City" = "#4DAF4A",
      "Zomba" = "#FF7F00"
    ),
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  labs(title = "Major Cities of Malawi")







Figure 21: Each highlighted district has its own colour, defined by a named character vector.

title: mwmap: A Complete Guide to Mapping Malawi in R
text:
4.3 mw_points() — plot geographic locations
mw_points() adds a layer of points to a map from a data frame containing longitude and latitude columns. Common uses include health facility locations, survey cluster coordinates, school or market sites, and infrastructure.
The lon and lat arguments are passed unquoted — like a tidyverse verb. The function converts the data frame to an sf object internally and uses geom_sf() so the coordinate system integrates correctly with the base map.
Important: when mapping a column to color or size, pass the column name as a quoted string — e.g. color = "facility_type", not color = facility_type. This is different from how mw_choropleth() works (which uses unquoted names), because mw_points() needs to handle both fixed values (e.g. color = "red") and column names in the same argument.

# Sample health facility data
facilities <- data.frame(
  name = c(
    "Kamuzu Central", "Queen Elizabeth Central", "Mzuzu Central","Zomba Central",
    "Dedza District", "Salima District", "Karonga District", "Mangochi District"),
  lon = c(33.780, 35.002, 34.018, 35.320, 34.339, 34.459, 33.930, 35.264),
  lat = c(-13.978, -15.785, -11.462, -15.380, -14.381, -13.782, -9.932, -14.477),
  level = c(
    "Central", "Central", "Central", "Central", "District", "District", "District", "District" ),
  beds = c(1200, 1350, 600, 450, 180, 160, 200, 210)
)


mw_map(fill_color = "#f5f5f5", border_color = "grey60", lakes = TRUE) +
  mw_points(
    facilities,
    lon,
    lat,
    color = "#E41A1C",
    size = 3,
    shape = 17 # 17 = filled triangle; 19 = filled circle
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Central Referral and District Hospitals",
    caption = "Source: Ministry of Health, Malawi (simulated)"
  )







Figure 22: Health facilities plotted as red triangles on a district base map.






4.3.1 Mapping point attributes to aesthetics
Pass a quoted column name to color or size to map a data attribute to a visual property. Then add a standard ggplot2 scale_color_manual() or scale_size_continuous() to control the exact colours and sizes used.

mw_map(fill_color = "#f0f4f8", border_color = "grey70", lakes = TRUE) +
  mw_points(
    facilities,
    lon,
    lat,
    color = "level", # quoted column name
    size = 3,
    alpha = 0.9
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Central" = "#E41A1C", "District" = "#1a5a9a"),
    name = "Facility Level"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Health Facilities by Level",
    subtitle = "Central and district hospitals"
  )







Figure 23: Facility level mapped to point colour. Central hospitals are shown in red, district hospitals in blue.







4.3.2 Labelling points
Set label = TRUE and provide the column name as a string to label_column to add text labels next to each point. Labels are automatically suppressed when they would overlap. For repelled, non-overlapping labels, use repel_labels = TRUE (requires the ggrepel package).

hospitals <- facilities[facilities$level == "Central", ]

mw_map(fill_color = "#f5f5f5", border_color = "grey70") +
  mw_points(
    hospitals,
    lon,
    lat,
    color = "#1a5a9a",
    size = 3,
    label = TRUE,
    label_column = "name", # column name as a quoted string
    label_size = 2.8,
    label_color = "#333333"
  ) +
  labs(title = "Central Hospitals — Malawi")







Figure 24: Central hospitals with name labels attached at point coordinates.

title: mwmap: A Complete Guide to Mapping Malawi in R
text:
4.4 mw_labels() — district name labels
mw_labels() adds district name text at the centroid of each polygon. It is the standalone version of the label_districts = TRUE argument in mw_map() and gives you more control: you can restrict labels to a subset of districts, change the font, and pass any additional arguments through to geom_sf_text().
The most useful arguments are:

districts — a character vector of district names to label. If NULL (default), all districts are labelled.
size — text size. The default of 3 works well for a full-country map.
color — text colour.
fontface — "plain", "bold", "italic", or "bold.italic".
label_column — column to use for the label text. Defaults to "ADM2_EN".


mw_map(fill_color = "#EDF8E9", border_color = "grey60") +
  mw_labels(
    size = 2.5,
    color = "#1a3a5c",
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  labs(title = "Malawi — All Districts Labelled")







Figure 25: All 28 districts labelled at their centroids.





A common pattern is to use mw_labels() to label only the specific districts you have highlighted, rather than all 28. This keeps the map clean while still giving the reader the names they need.

mw_map(
  highlight_districts = c("Lilongwe", "Blantyre", "Mzuzu City", "Zomba"),
  highlight_fill = "#FEEDDE",
  highlight_border_color = "#E6550D",
  fill_color = "#f7f7f7",
  border_color = "grey70"
) +
  mw_labels(
    districts = c("Lilongwe", "Blantyre", "Mzuzu City", "Zomba"),
    size = 3.5,
    color = "#E6550D",
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  labs(title = "Major Cities of Malawi")







Figure 26: Labels only on the four highlighted cities. Restricting labels to highlighted districts avoids clutter.

text:
5.2 Using scale_fill_mw()
scale_fill_mw() is a ggplot2 scale function — drop it into any pipeline using +, just like scale_fill_distiller() or scale_fill_viridis_c().
The key arguments:

palette — the name of a palette from get_mw_palettes(). Default: "health".
discrete — set TRUE for categorical data (factors). Default: FALSE (continuous gradient).
reverse — TRUE flips the palette direction. Useful when the default direction (light = low, dark = high) does not suit your variable.
name — the legend title.
na.value — colour for missing data. Defaults to "grey50".

joined <- mw_join(health_data, quiet = TRUE)

mw_map(data = joined, fill = "rate_per_1000") +
  scale_fill_mw("health", name = "Rate") +
  labs(title = '"health"')

mw_map(data = joined, fill = "rate_per_1000") +
  scale_fill_mw("malaria", name = "Rate") +
  labs(title = '"malaria"')

mw_map(data = joined, fill = "rate_per_1000") +
  scale_fill_mw("poverty", name = "Rate") +
  labs(title = '"poverty"')









Figure 28: Three palettes applied to the same incidence rate data. The palette choice substantially changes the visual impression.











Figure 29: Three palettes applied to the same incidence rate data. The palette choice substantially changes the visual impression.











Figure 30: Three palettes applied to the same incidence rate data. The palette choice substantially changes the visual impression.







5.2.1 Reversing a palette
Some variables make more intuitive sense when the colour direction is flipped. For example, a “coverage” metric where higher is better might read more naturally if the dark end of the palette represents high coverage (good) rather than the default where dark typically implies high risk or high burden.

mw_map(data = joined, fill = "rate_per_1000") +
  scale_fill_mw("malaria", reverse = TRUE, name = "Rate per 1,000") +
  labs(title = "Reversed palette: dark = low, light = high")







Figure 31: The malaria palette reversed. Now lighter colour = higher value.







5.2.2 Extracting hex codes with get_mw_palette()
You can extract the raw hex codes from any palette for use outside of ggplot2 — in tables, slide decks, custom charts, or base R plots. The n argument interpolates the palette to exactly n colours, which is useful when you need more or fewer colours than the palette’s default length.

# All colours in the three-colour 'regions' palette
get_mw_palette("regions")
#> [1] "#E41A1C" "#377EB8" "#4DAF4A"
#> [1] "#E41A1C" "#377EB8" "#4DAF4A"

# Interpolate to exactly 7 colours from the 'health' palette
get_mw_palette("health", n = 7)
#> [1] "#E8F4F8" "#BCDEED" "#8EC8E5" "#5EB4E0" "#3C98D0" "#267AB8" "#1A5A9A"

# Reverse the malaria palette
get_mw_palette("malaria", reverse = TRUE)
#> [1] "#A63603" "#E6550D" "#FD8D3C" "#FDBE85" "#FEEDDE"

# All 28 districts, sorted alphabetically
mw_districts()

text:
7.2 Standardising names with mw_clean_names()
mw_clean_names() applies a series of transformations to bring district name strings closer to the shapefile format:

Converts to title case ("lilongwe" → "Lilongwe")
Strips trailing “District”, “T/A”, “TA” ("Blantyre District" → "Blantyre")
Normalises whitespace (collapses multiple spaces to one)
Applies known shapefile variant mappings:

"Nkhata Bay" → "Nkhatabay" (the shapefile omits the space)
"Mzuzu" → "Mzuzu City" (common shorthand → full shapefile name)



messy <- c("lilongwe", "BLANTYRE DISTRICT", "nkhata bay", "mzuzu", "zomba")
mw_clean_names(messy)
#> [1] "Lilongwe"   "Blantyre"   "Nkhatabay"  "Mzuzu City" "Zomba"
#> [1] "Lilongwe"   "Blantyre"   "Nkhatabay"  "Mzuzu City" "Zomba"

mw_join() calls mw_clean_names() on your district column automatically, so in normal use you never need to call this function yourself. But calling it explicitly before a join lets you inspect what the cleaning will do to your data before committing to the join.

title: mwmap: A Complete Guide to Mapping Malawi in R
text:
7.3 Finding close matches with mw_suggest_matches()
When mw_join() reports unmatched districts, mw_suggest_matches() helps you figure out the correct name. It uses Levenshtein edit distance to find the most similar names in the candidate list — the same algorithm used by autocorrect. The first suggestion is almost always the intended match when you have a simple typo.

# A simple typo — one extra "e"
mw_suggest_matches("Lilongwee", mw_districts())
#> [1] "Lilongwe"      "Lilongwe City" "Blantyre"
#> [1] "Lilongwe"  "Salima"   "Likoma"

# Another typo
mw_suggest_matches("Blantyree", mw_districts())
#> [1] "Blantyre"      "Blantyre City" "Mulanje"
#> [1] "Blantyre"  "Balaka"   "Salima"







WarningTwo name variants to always watch for






What you might write
Correct shapefile name




"Nkhata Bay"
"Nkhatabay"


"Mzuzu"
"Mzuzu City"



mw_clean_names() and mw_join() handle both automatically. But if you are writing district names directly as strings in mw_highlight(districts = ...) or mw_labels(districts = ...), use the shapefile form (right column). Check the exact names with mw_districts().

title: mwmap: A Complete Guide to Mapping Malawi in R
text:
8.1 Example 1 — Malaria burden map
This example builds a complete publication-ready map that combines a categorical choropleth, lake overlay, outline highlights on the major cities, and text labels. The key insight is that each element is a separate layer added with +, and the final mw_layout() call applies consistent titling and styling to the whole figure.

# Step 1: classify districts into burden tiers
health_data$burden <- cut(
  health_data$rate_per_1000,
  breaks = c(0, 3, 5, 8, 12, Inf),
  labels = c("Minimal", "Low", "Moderate", "High", "Critical"),
  ordered_result = TRUE
)

# Step 2: join to geometry
map_df <- mw_join(health_data, quiet = TRUE)

# Step 3: build the map layer by layer
mw_map(
  data = map_df,
  fill = "burden",
  lakes = TRUE,
  border_color = "white",
  border_size = 0.4
) +
  scale_fill_mw(
    "malaria",
    discrete = TRUE,
    name = "Burden Level",
    na.value = "grey85"
  ) +
  mw_highlight(
    districts = c("Blantyre", "Lilongwe"),
    outline_only = TRUE,
    color = "#333333",
    size = 1
  ) +
  mw_labels(
    districts = c("Blantyre", "Lilongwe", "Mzuzu City", "Zomba"),
    size = 3,
    color = "#333333"
  ) +
  mw_layout(
    title = "Malaria Burden Classification by District",
    subtitle = "Malawi · District Level · Simulated data · 2024",
    caption = "Source: Simulated data · Visualisation: mwmap package",
    legend_position = "right"
  )







Figure 33: A complete, multi-layer malaria burden map suitable for publication.

title: mwmap: A Complete Guide to Mapping Malawi in R
text:
8.2 Example 2 — Regional vaccination coverage
This example uses mw_regions() to show a regional-level indicator. The darker the green, the higher the vaccination coverage. We encode the coverage values by manually mapping each region to a colour from the "vaccination" palette — darker for higher coverage. The result communicates both geography and relative performance at a glance.

mw_regions(
  region_colors = c(
    "Northern" = "#31A354", # highest coverage → darkest green
    "Central" = "#74C476",
    "Southern" = "#C7E9C0" # lowest coverage → lightest green
  ),
  labels = TRUE,
  label_size = 5,
  label_face = "bold",
  lakes = TRUE
) +
  mw_layout(
    title = "Childhood Vaccination Coverage by Region",
    subtitle = "Malawi · Simulated estimates · 2024",
    caption = "Darker green = higher coverage · Source: Simulated"
  )







Figure 34: Vaccination coverage at the regional level. Darker green = higher coverage.

title: mwmap: A Complete Guide to Mapping Malawi in R
section: 8.3 Example 3 — Infrastructure overlaid on burden data
text:
8.3 Example 3 — Infrastructure overlaid on burden data
This example combines two data sources on a single map: the district-level health burden (continuous choropleth) and the locations of health facilities (points coloured by facility level). This dual-layer approach allows the reader to see both the health burden and the distribution of health infrastructure simultaneously — and to immediately spot areas where burden is high but facilities are sparse.

mw_map(
  data = map_df,
  fill = "rate_per_1000",
  lakes = TRUE,
  border_color = "white",
  border_size = 0.3
) +
  scale_fill_mw(
    "health",
    name = "Rate per 1,000",
    na.value = "grey85"
  ) +
  mw_points(
    facilities,
    lon,
    lat,
    color = "level",
    size = 3,
    alpha = 0.9
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Central" = "#E41A1C", "District" = "#1a5a9a"),
    name = "Facility Level"
  ) +
  mw_layout(
    title = "Health Facilities and Malaria Burden",
    subtitle = "Malawi · 2024 · Simulated data",
    caption = "Blue = district hospitals · Red = central referral hospitals",
    legend_position = "right"
  )







Figure 35: Health burden choropleth with facility locations overlaid. High-burden areas with few facilities become immediately visible.

title: mwmap: A Complete Guide to Mapping Malawi in R
text:
8.4 Example 4 — Traditional authority detail
This example zooms into a single district (Lilongwe) to show the TA-level structure. This kind of map is useful for district health offices, local programme teams, and field research that needs to operate at the sub-district level. The thick district boundary provides a frame of reference; the TA name labels let the reader identify each sub-unit by name.

mw_ta_map(
  districts = "Lilongwe",
  fill = "white",
  border_color = "grey80",
  border_size = 0.2,
  district_border = TRUE,
  district_border_color = "#E41A1C",
  district_border_size = 1.2,
  labels = TRUE,
  label_size = 2.2,
  label_color = "#333333"
) +
  mw_layout(
    title = "Traditional Authorities — Lilongwe District",
    caption = "Source: MASDAP · mwmap package"
  )







Figure 36: Traditional Authorities in Lilongwe district. The thick red border is the district boundary; thin grey lines are TA boundaries.
